A_target.statement:
Let $B$ be a [[Definition:Boolean Algebra|Boolean algebra]].
A [[Definition:Filter on Boolean Algebra|filter]] $F$ on $B$ is a subset such that:
:$a \in F \land a \le b \implies b \in F$
:$a, b \in F \implies a \wedge b \in F$
and the [[Definition:Ultrafilter|ultrafilters]] are the maximal proper filters.

B_source.statement:
Let $B$ be a [[Definition:Boolean Algebra|Boolean algebra]].
An [[Definition:Ideal (Order Theory)|ideal]] $I$ on $B$ is a subset such that:
:$b \in I \land a \le b \implies a \in I$
:$a, b \in I \implies a \vee b \in I$
and the maximal proper ideals are the [[Definition:Prime Ideal (Order Theory)|prime ideals]].

substitutions.the ideal: its complement, which is a filter

derived.the quotient by an ideal: the quotient by the corresponding filter, giving the same algebra

validity_conditions: Complementation in a Boolean algebra is an order-reversing involution, so it carries ideals to filters and back exactly.
Closure under finite joins becomes closure under finite meets under the involution, and properness is preserved.
In a general lattice without complements the two notions are order-dual but not related by an explicit involution, so the correspondence is a duality of definitions rather than a bijection.
proof_plan: Let $I$ be an [[Definition:Ideal (Order Theory)|ideal]] and let $F = \set {\neg a: a \in I}$.
Complementation is [[Definition:Order-Reversing Mapping|order-reversing]], so downward closure of $I$ becomes upward closure of $F$.

By [[De Morgan's Laws (Boolean Algebras)|De Morgan's laws]]:
:$
eg a \wedge 
eg b = 
eg \paren {a \vee b}$
so closure under finite joins becomes closure under finite meets.
